title: Tu B'Av (Mishnah Taanit 4:8)
hookLine: six days after the saddest day comes a day of love, when young women danced in the vineyards
tomorrow: Year two close: the whole Torah

lines: SIX DAYS AFTER THE SADDEST DAY.
cards: There were no happier days for Israel than the fifteenth of Av and Yom Kippur. That's the claim, near the end of a Mishnah tractate about fasts, in the name of a sage called Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel. Yom Kippur?
The day of not eating, of standing all day in white? Happy? And the fifteenth of Av, a quiet midsummer date, sits just six days after the day Jerusalem is mourned on the floor.

teach.b: Tu B'Av means the fifteenth of Av: fifteen is written tet and vav, nine and six, which together sound like tu. Then the Mishnah tells what happened.
On those two days the daughters of Jerusalem went out in white, and every dress was borrowed.

Even the king's daughter borrowed from the high priest's daughter, and the high priest's daughter from the next family down, so no girl without a fine dress would be put to shame. Nobody could tell whose family was rich.
They danced in the vineyards, calling to the young men: lift your eyes and see whom you choose. The Mishnah doesn't say why either day was so happy; the Talmud fills that in.
Yom Kippur is easy: it was the day of forgiveness. For Tu B'Av it collects several reasons. On this day, it says, the tribes were first allowed to marry one another.
The tribe of Benjamin, cut off after a terrible civil war in the book of Judges, was let back in. Some say the generation dying in the wilderness stopped dying.
And the cutting of wood for the altar ended for the year, as the summer sun weakened.
Most of the reasons are about a door opening: between tribes, back into a family, out of a long sentence.
The calendar puts the two days side by side: first the floor, the candle and the cry of how; six days later, white dresses and dancing.
Mourning gets its full day, and then the same month turns. In Israel today, Tu B'Av has come back as a day of love: weddings, flowers, songs on the radio.

how: Tu B'Av, the fifteenth of Av, has no fixed rituals in Jewish law beyond omitting some penitential prayers; in modern Israel it is celebrated as a day of love, popular for weddings, parties and romance.

games.q: you're the king's daughter on the fifteenth of Av, and you own the finest white dress in Jerusalem. what do you wear?
o: a dress borrowed from the high priest's daughter.
games.why: in the Mishnah, even the king's daughter borrows, so no girl without a fine dress is put to shame.

practice: Bring one person to mind, a partner, a friend, a child, a parent, someone who has stood by you in a hard stretch, and picture their face.
Think of one thing about them you've never quite said out loud, something they do that makes your life lighter, and hold the person and the thing together, the way you'd hold a gift before giving it.
